comparator.name: Environmental Sciences
comparator.sourceNotes: The current 180-EC programme comprises a 120-EC common part, a 30-EC specialisation and 30 EC of free choice. The common part includes 105 EC of credited compulsory courses, a 3-EC mathematics/statistics choice and a 12-EC thesis. The broad Interdisciplinary Environmental Challenges specialisation is reconstructed with its required nexus course, two social-science options and two natural-science/technology selections in official order. Required non-credit safety modules are acknowledged but not encoded as credit-bearing components.

alternatives.labelRationale: This curriculum centres biodiversity, conservation, ecosystem processes, environmental quality, soils, water and ecological resilience while retaining climate and Earth-system foundations.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: This route makes ecosystem condition, biodiversity, conservation and resilience the organising priority. Relative to the closest programme it replaces programming, mathematical and data-analysis courses with conservation, evolution, life-science and marine-ecology study; the pair differs by six courses and 45 EC in each direction.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest programme integrates environmental systems, climate, pollution, quantitative evidence and sustainable solutions. Environmental quality/ecosystem resilience and environmental policy/governance form two further evidenced, coherent and mechanically feasible directions. They are pairwise distinct by at least 45 EC, so production stops at the three-alternative maximum.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both develop transferable research and professional skills; WUR focuses them specifically on environmental inquiry.
Both establish systems foundations for sustainability problems and solutions.
Both examine environmental systems and solution design; WUR provides dedicated technology training.
Both develop mathematical methods used in quantitative environmental analysis.
Both provide biological foundations relevant to environmental microbiology and organism–environment interactions; WUR adds dedicated toxicology.
UCR has environmental chemistry within advanced courses but no selected introductory general-chemistry equivalent.
UCR lacks a separate second general-chemistry component in these pathways.
UCR supplies quantitative foundations elsewhere, but no additional selected row is presented as equivalent to this restricted introductory choice.
Both examine Earth-system change; WUR provides a broader dedicated climate-system component.
Both integrate evidence across linked socio-environmental or Earth-system processes, with different disciplinary scope.
Both address atmospheric change and environmental consequences; WUR adds dedicated air-quality science.
Both examine chemical and biogeochemical processes in soils and connected environmental systems.
Both examine renewable energy systems and their sustainable design.
UCR lacks a selected dedicated organic-chemistry foundation equivalent to this requirement.
Both establish ecological and biodiversity foundations.
Both analyse interactions and trade-offs among environmental pressures and ecological systems.
Both analyse soils, aquifers and water systems; WUR provides a more dedicated water-analysis sequence.
Both examine water systems, management and environmental consequences.
Both apply environmental chemistry to contamination, resource recovery and remediation; WUR focuses on organic chemistry.
Both provide probability and statistical inference for environmental evidence.
Both use computational and numerical modelling for complex environmental processes.
Both use geospatial observation and evidence to analyse environmental change.
Both develop applied environmental research and collaborative project skills.
UCR includes applied research, but no further selected course reproduces this 12-EC international environmental project.
The WUR thesis is a required independent environmental-sciences research project; UCR optional independent research is shown in parallel as a comparison-only opportunity.
Both examine the institutions and governance of sustainability transitions.
Both analyse policy systems and institutional responses; WUR integrates environmental economics and law.
Microeconomics supplies the economic decision framework that WUR applies directly to environmental problems.
Both examine international production, exchange and their wider consequences; WUR centres environmental effects.
UCR covers politics and governance but lacks a selected specialist international and EU environmental-law course.
WUR retains a full 30-EC free-choice semester; UCR flexibility is expressed through the complete selected 180-EC programmes rather than a separate unassigned semester.

notes.text: WUR provides a prescribed environmental-sciences sequence in chemistry, pollution modelling, air quality, environmental technology, policy, economics and law, followed by a formal specialisation and thesis. UCR can combine substantial environmental science, ecology, climate, data, governance and sustainability study, but does not reproduce the same specialist laboratory, engineering or environmental-law sequence.
